name: Signal Green
lede: Signal green is a deep, cool green named for the go-ahead light of traffic signals, and also the name of a fluorescent Day-Glo pigment.

sections.title: Go
sections.body:
Paterson defines the green light as a signal, green in color, that it is in order to proceed, as on traffic lights, and as a sign to go ahead with any course of action [1]. The same dictionary notes that the Green Line dividing Nicosia since December 1963 was so called because British authorities used green ink on the map [1].

Livingstone names Signal Green as one of six Day-Glo pigments, the others being Saturn Green, Arc Yellow, Blaze Orange, Rocket Red and Neon Red [2]. Such a pigment reflects more light in some wavebands than white paper does, and relatively less in the shorter wavebands, which supply the energy it converts into its own glow [2]. The Day-Glo pigment is a bright fluorescent green, so the screen swatch here, a calmer deep green, stands for the signal use rather than the pigment [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 8 works [3]. Two are Félix Vallotton's *Corn Fields* of 1900 and Franz Marc's *Weasels at Play* of 1911 [3]. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [3].

origin.source: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour, p. 197; Livingstone, Vision and Art, ch. 10
